questions.question: Galileo Galilei timed bronze balls rolling down grooves cut in wooden ramps. He reasoned that a ball rolling down one ramp and up a second one climbs almost back to its starting height, however steep the second ramp is. Then he asked what the ball would do if the second ramp were laid flat and perfectly smooth. What did he conclude?
questions.answer: It would roll on forever at the same speed
choices: It would roll on forever at the same speed
It would slow down with no slope to push it
It would stop as soon as it reached the flat
It would keep speeding up along the flat
questions.context: On a flat second ramp the ball could never climb back to its starting height, so Galileo concluded that it would roll on and on without slowing: nothing is needed to keep a moving thing moving. Real balls stop because friction and the air push against them, which is why a ball rolled across grass stops far sooner than one on smooth ice. Aristotle had taught that a pushed thing stops once nothing pushes it, and many people still picture a push that slowly wears off.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade lessons on the first law open with Galileo's ramps and his conclusion that a moving body keeps moving unless friction stops it.

questions.question: Isaac Newton set out his first law of motion, often called the law of inertia, in his book the Principia in 1687. Centuries later, a space probe far out between the stars, with no star or planet anywhere near it, shuts off its engines. What happens to its motion after that?
questions.answer: It keeps moving straight on at the same speed
choices: It keeps moving straight on at the same speed
It keeps going, but slower and slower until it stops
It stops at once, with no engine to push it
It speeds up, with no air to hold it back
questions.context: With almost no force acting on it, the probe goes on in a straight line at the same speed, as Newton's first law says; it needs its engines only to speed up, slow down or turn. On Earth moving things stop because friction and the air push against them, but out between the stars there is nothing to rub against.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade states Newton's first law and applies it to motion with no unbalanced force, the spacecraft coasting in space being the standard case.

questions.question: Aboard a space station in orbit, a big steel toolbox and a pencil float side by side, and a bathroom scale would read nothing for either of them. An astronaut gives each one a shove to send it drifting across the cabin. What will she find?
questions.answer: The toolbox is far harder to set moving
choices: The toolbox is far harder to set moving
Both are equally easy, since neither has weight
The toolbox is harder, but only by a little
The pencil is harder to set moving
questions.context: Floating things in orbit show no weight on a scale, but they keep all their mass, and mass is what gives a thing its inertia: the more mass, the harder it is to start, stop or turn. A NASA lesson makes the same point with an astronaut struggling to push a one-ton satellite out of a space shuttle's cargo bay.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that more mass means more inertia, and that mass, unlike weight, stays the same in orbit.

questions.question: A driver slams on the brakes, and her car jolts to a stop. Her passenger, who has not buckled his seat belt, lurches forward toward the dashboard. Why does he lurch forward?
questions.answer: His body goes on moving as the car stops
choices: His body goes on moving as the car stops
The braking car throws him forward
The seat behind him pushes him forward
The air in the car rushes forward with him
questions.context: He was moving at the car's speed, and the brakes slow only the car, so his body goes on moving until something stops it: the dashboard or the windshield, if he is not buckled in. A seat belt gives the force that slows him along with the car, spread across the strong bones of the hips and shoulder. Nothing throws him forward; the car simply stops beneath him.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade first-law lessons explain why seat belts are needed: passengers keep moving forward when a car stops suddenly.

questions.question: A car swings left around a sharp bend at a steady speed. A box of apples on the back seat slides across to the right and bumps against the right-hand door. Why does the box slide to the right?
questions.answer: It goes on straight while the car turns
choices: It goes on straight while the car turns
An outward force flings it away from the bend
Its weight pulls it to the outside of the bend
The turning car pushes it toward the door
questions.context: The box keeps moving in a straight line while the car turns left beneath it, so the right-hand door swings round to meet it; the seat's grip is too weak to turn the box with the car. Passengers feel flung outward on a bend for the same reason, and the outward force they seem to feel is not a real push from anything.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade applies the first law to a change of direction: a thing goes on in a straight line unless a force turns it.

questions.question: A magician sets plates and glasses on a smooth silk cloth, meaning to pull the cloth out and leave them standing on the table. He can tug the cloth slowly, or yank it away in a split second. Which pull leaves the dishes in place, and why?
questions.answer: The yank, as friction has little time to act
choices: The yank, as friction has little time to act
The slow tug, as it drags on the dishes less
Either one, as inertia holds the dishes still
Neither, as the cloth always drags the dishes
questions.context: The cloth rubs on the dishes either way, but in a split-second yank that friction acts for so short a time that it barely moves them, and their inertia keeps them almost where they were. A slow tug gives friction time to drag them off with the cloth. Inertia is not a grip that holds things still; it is only their resistance to a change in motion.
questions.grade_note: The tablecloth pulled from under the dishes is a classroom demonstration of the first law that seventh-grade lessons use.

questions.question: A girl whirls a ball on a string in a flat circle above her head. Partway round, the string snaps. Seen from directly above, what path does the ball take as it flies away?
questions.answer: A straight line, the way it was heading
choices: A straight line, the way it was heading
A curve that keeps bending round and round
A straight line directly out away from her
A spiral that slowly widens out from her
questions.context: The string's pull was all that bent the ball's path into a circle, so once it snaps the ball goes on in a straight line in the direction it was moving at that instant, along the edge of the circle. In studies in the 1980s, many college students expected a ball let go from a curved path to keep curving, an idea much like the old theory of impetus.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the first law's motion is in a straight line, so a thing freed from a circle flies off straight.

questions.question: A boy sits on a train gliding along a straight, level track at a steady speed. He tosses a ball straight up above his lap, and while it is in the air the train rolls on down the track. Where does the ball come down?
choices: Back in his hand
A little way behind him
A little way ahead of him
Behind him, as far as the train has gone
questions.context: The ball was already moving forward with the train when it left his hand, and nothing pushes it backward, so it keeps the train's speed and stays above his hand all the way up and down. Galileo argued the same in his Dialogue of 1632 about a cannonball dropped from the top of a smoothly sailing ship's mast: it falls at the foot of the mast, not behind it.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade applies the first law to a moving vehicle: anything inside it keeps the vehicle's motion until a force changes it.

questions.question: The iron head of a carpenter's hammer has worked loose on its wooden handle. He holds the hammer upright, head on top, and strikes the bottom end of the handle hard on a concrete floor. The head slides a little farther down the handle and sits tighter. Why?
questions.answer: The handle stops, but the head keeps going
choices: The handle stops, but the head keeps going
The jolt from the floor drives the head down
Gravity pulls harder on the head at the jolt
The heavy head falls faster than the handle
questions.context: Head and handle move down together until the handle hits the floor and stops short; the head, with only the wood's friction to stop it, keeps moving and slides farther on. The floor pushes up, and only on the handle, so it cannot be what drives the head down. Heavy and light things fall alike, and here nothing is falling freely in any case.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade explains everyday cases with the first law: a moving thing keeps moving when what carries it stops.

questions.question: Johannes Kepler coined the word inertia from a Latin word meaning idle or sluggish. Isaac Newton later built his first law of motion on the idea. In Newton's physics, what does a body's inertia do?
questions.answer: It resists any change in the body's motion
choices: It resists any change in the body's motion
It makes a moving body slow down and then stop
It pushes a moving body to keep it going
It pulls the body down toward the ground
questions.context: Inertia is a body's resistance to any change in its motion, whether starting, stopping, speeding up or turning, and the more mass it has, the more inertia. Kepler, who took rest to be natural, meant only a resistance to being moved; for Newton, inertia also keeps a moving body moving. It is not a force that pushes, and the pull toward the ground is gravity.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names inertia as the resistance to a change in motion that Newton's first law describes.
